key_insight: A near-singular Navier–Stokes-like flow can drive magnetic reconnection that splits a flux ring into multiple daughter rings, with the reconnection pathway shaped by Lorentz feedback and asymmetry in the imposed swirl.
engineering_relevance: This suggests that extreme fluid strain and swirl in plasma- or MHD-like systems can trigger abrupt magnetic topology changes, which is important for predicting stability in fusion, space, and astrophysical flows.
method: Simulated resistive magnetohydrodynamics with a magnetic ring driven by a regularized imposed flow that matches the collapsing-core geometry and scaling.
Released the drive at the nominal singular time and followed free evolution to observe reconnection, splitting, and merging.
Compared 2D/3D behavior and used normal-form analysis (pitchfork-to-fold, cusp) to interpret bifurcation asymmetry.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical MHD simulations in 2D and 3D showing pre- and post-release reconnections that split the ring and persist in three dimensions, with cusp normal form matching the single-island asymmetry without adjustable parameters.
watch_item: The result comes from a designed, regularized forcing and numerical simulations, so the physical relevance depends on how closely the imposed flow and resistive parameters match a real singular-flow scenario.
paper_title: Magnetic flux ring splitting near a Navier-Stokes singularity
